requirement: Emitted objects reject an undocumented property, so a credential, a raw upstream body or a filesystem path cannot ride out to the browser in a catch-all field.
why_it_matters: SHARED wire decision 8: raw platform objects, credentials, filesystem paths and arbitrary pane targets never become browser-controlled arguments. Strictness is the mechanism — every emitted object is additionalProperties:false, so the leak fails at the schema instead of shipping. §1's ignore-unknown-fields rule is a runtime courtesy between client and server, not a licence for the artifact these tests pin.

value.detail: the configured workspace key was rejected

assert.note: the sentence names the problem, never the URL that carries the key

documents.name: a service entry says what it knows without naming where it lives

value.detail: no workspace profile is configured for this project

assert.note: never reached is different from reached and down

counterexamples.name: a credential in a service error
counterexamples.why: The single most damaging leak in the product: a secret reaching a browser page over a loopback API that any local process can read. Strict objects are what stop it, which is why no emitted schema may ever relax additionalProperties.

counterexamples.name: a raw upstream body kept as a catch-all
counterexamples.why: "Keep the original response in case we need it" is how a trace tree, an internal account id and a key reference reach the page. The adapter normalises into the documented fields; whatever it did not model is dropped, not smuggled.

counterexamples.name: a filesystem path on an operation target
counterexamples.why: The target echoes back only ids the caller already named. A path invites a client to start sending one, which is the first step toward a browser-chosen target.

counterexamples.name: an extra field on an emitted Receipt
counterexamples.why: The receipt already says what happened in `detail`. A machine-readable pane target is an argument the browser could learn and replay, and arbitrary pane targets are exactly what SHARED forbids.

counterexamples.name: an undocumented field on a 1.4 request
counterexamples.why: Requests are strict so that a security invariant is never inferred from an unknown field. Ignoring `as_user` would be safe today and load-bearing the moment someone implements it; rejecting it keeps the decision explicit.
